newsitem.title: CHINA: U.S. tells China of need to cut trade surplus.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tells China of need to cut trade surplus.

text.p: (Corrects headline and first paragraph to read "trade surplus", not "trade deficit")
China needs to cut its mounting trade surplus with the United States, and a "fair share" of contracts for American firms would help to close the gap, a senior U.S. trade official said on Tuesday.
"The trade deficit with China is not politically sustainable and needs to be addressed," Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat told reporters.
Eizenstat said that in talks with Chinese officials he delivered this message along with a list of major projects on which U.S. companies hope to win contracts.
He did not name any of the companies but he said they ranged from aviation to energy and telecommunications, and contracts could be worth tens of billions of dollars.
The American official has been seen as pushing for contracts that could be signed during Vice President Al Gore's visit to China this month.
The U.S. deficit with China swelled to nearly $40 billion last year, up 17 percent over 1995 and a fourfold rise since 1990, according to U.S. statistics.
China accounted for almost 24 percent of the global U.S. trade deficit last year, and was rapidly replacing Japan as the main trade concern in Congress, Eizenstat said.
The U.S. official said that concerns would ease if U.S. companies won a "fair share" of some $700 billion China would spend on infrastructure projects over the next 10 years.
China disputes the U.S. trade data, saying it had a $10 billion surplus with the United States last year. Its figures exclude trade through the British colony of Hong Kong.
But Eizenstat, speaking to reporters before leaving for China's financial heart of Shanghai, said Chinese officials signalled some understanding of the sensitivity of the trade issue in congress.
Eizenstat repeated Washington's support for China's bid to join the the World Trade Organisation but only on acceptable terms.
Beijing wants to join on easier terms of a developing country but Washington insists the Chinese economy is too big for such treatment.
"We need sound, commercially viable terms," he said, adding that some 30 other states were looking to join the international body and were watching the negotiations with Beijing closely.
China also needed to give so-called national treatment to foreign companies and remove hidden obstacles to businesses, the official said.
Beijing has frequently said that a lack of U.S. government financing was holding back U.S. exports to China.
Eizenstat said the U.S. Export-Import Bank would soon post a lending officer to the American embassy in Beijing in a bid to reduce that disadvantage.
